newsitem.title: CUBA: Castro says Cuba will keep one-party system.
newsitem.headline: Castro says Cuba will keep one-party system.

text.p: President Fidel Castro, clearly encouraged by recent Cuban diplomatic successes, has rejected foreign calls for political reforms and insisted that his country will keep its one-party communist system.

Castro, who turned 70 this year, made a spirited defence of Cuba's political system during a speech on Saturday night to a Havana Communist Party meeting in which he declared, "I'm proud to be a communist" and "Nothing is possible without socialism."
The Cuban leader was categoric in his negative reponse to recent calls by some foreign governments other than the United States, notably Spain, for Cuba to adopt a multi-party system.

"To those who tell us that we should divide ourselves into fragments, we say no. If they ask us to create 25 parties, we say no," Castro said. "The party which directs the Revolution is enough and we don't need more, because it guarantees the unity, future and independence of our country," he added.
"We won't kneel before anyone, nor will we seek charity from anyone," the Cuban leader said. Excerpts from the 1 1/2 hour speech were quoted by Cuban state media on Sunday.

Castro's words were a clear rejection of an initiative by Spain's conservative government to persuade the European Union (EU) to place conditions on future EU economic cooperation with Cuba. Madrid is calling for democratic reforms and faster economic liberalisation on the communist-ruled island.

Castro said Cuba "has more friends than ever." He mentioned a recent overwhelming United Nations General Assembly vote of 137 to 3 in favour of a Cuban resolution calling for the lifting of the 34-year-old U.S. economic embargo against Cuba.

Other Cuban diplomatic successes this month include a similar anti-embargo call issued by leaders from Latin America, Spain and Portugal and a meeting between Castro and Pope John Paul II in Rome in which the Cuban leader thanked the Vatican for its support against the U.S. embargo policy.

In his speech, Castro again repeated his rejection of a personal call for political change in Cuba made by Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar. When the two met at the Ibero- American summit in Chile this month, Aznar, using the image of a chess game, urged the Cuban leader to "make a move."
"I told him that the destiny of a country is not played out in a chess game," Castro said, sarcastically referring to the Spanish leader as "this little gentleman."

He also underlined Cuba's socialist option in economic policy. He said Cuba's opening to foreign investment was part of a tactical move to help the island emerge from a five-year economic recession triggered by the collapse of Cuba's trade and aid ties with the former Soviet bloc.
"But socialism remains the strategy," Castro added.

He repeated an official forecast that the Cuban economy would grow by 7 percent this year, despite problems like the U.S. Helms-Burton law, which targets foreign investment in Cuba, and Hurricane Lili, which battered west and central provinces of the island on Oct. 17 and 18. Castro said Lili caused some $500 million worth of damage but gave no details.

The Cuban leader jokingly suggested sending a telegram to the Republican sponsors of the Helms-Burton law, Sen. Jesse Helms and Congressman Dan Burton, to inform them that their law had helped to unite international opposition against the tightened U.S. embargo on Cuba.
